title: Dumbbell rows Tutorial for a Bigger Back
summary: NH explains how and why he does dumbbell rows: beginners should start with unsupported two-arm bent-over rows to learn to use the lower back as a stable bridge, then progress to bench-supported one-arm rows standing on both feet. He covers back movement versus arm pulling, neutral vs pronated grips, avoiding supinated grips, strap use, and prioritising the stretch.
claims: Beginners should not use a support when rowing; they must first learn to stabilise with the lower back and hamstrings
Unsupported two-arm dumbbell rows build coordination, hamstring mobility and spinal rigidity that carry over to deadlifts and barbell rows
He did unsupported dumbbell rows daily for four years when starting, because he had no bench and a fragile floor
People who can't feel their upper back in rows use the lower back and posterior chain as a mover instead of a bridge, fatiguing it while the upper back stays untouched
A more parallel torso gives more stretch and more lat involvement; a more upright torso shifts work to the upper back and traps
He now does about 70% of his dumbbell rows supported on a bench and 30% unsupported
Never put your knee on the bench when rowing; stand on both feet, staggered stance is fine
Kneeling on the bench risks torsion and damage to the core and lower back, and standing has carryover to other lifts
Standing rows make form deteriorate before an injury occurs, which is a safety feature
Establish position before pulling: back neutral or tall, never rounded, arm fully extended
A tight straight arm at the start lets you pull with the back, the same logic as deadlifts
On the descent the back should move and stretch with the weight; if only the arm moves it's a hammer curl
Ignore people calling back movement in rows body English; without movement and stretch of the upper back you're not training it
Keep the body rigid: no knee flexion, hip flexion or torso-angle shifts, otherwise you're doing a one-arm deadlift working the erectors
With a neutral grip, aim the dumbbell toward the ground with a slight twist toward the body, then pull up and squeeze
With a pronated grip the dumbbell can travel forward in a pendulum arc, adding extra stretch tension on the upper back
Use both neutral and pronated grips for overuse-injury prevention and complete upper-back training; they can be supersetted without much mutual fatigue
Never use supinated grips for rows, shrugs or deadlifts, and never use mixed grip as a bodybuilder; biceps can't handle what the back can and risk tearing
Use straps only when you can't grip the weight; overusing them steals forearm work
With dumbbells, straps limit wrist rotation, which can disrupt the path or muscle recruitment
Straps are necessary for shrugs and deadlifts but not for rows
Rows hit the upper back without taxing the lower back much, which is essential for naturals since the lower back limits upper-back growth
Do rows once or twice a week for 8-12 reps, focusing on the stretch
If forced to choose between the squeeze at the top and the stretch at the bottom, prioritise the stretch
exercises: hip hinge, flatten back, row without letting go
teaches using lower back as a bridge; beginner variation
both feet on floor, staggered stance, arm straight at start, back moves with the weight
